claims.text: The lower-adjoined family generates \(J_v\), and the 2024 theorem proves its minimality over \(\mathbb Z\). [doi:10.1112/jlms.12832, lines 213-235]
The claimed no-syzygy theorem is deduced from Theorem 4.4; it is the essential input used to upgrade minimal generation to integral independence. [doi:10.1112/jlms.12832, lines 790-831]

Assuming that no-syzygy theorem, the lower-adjoined residues are an integral homogeneous basis of \(J_v/A_+J_v\): a homogeneous kernel relation is exactly a prohibited syzygy; hence no torsion remains. The grading is Schur degree (ordinary cohomological degrees are twice these).

The first missing certificate is the large-\(N\) descent in Theorem 4.4: one needs \[ P\bigl(\operatorname{Lin}_{\widehat\varphi}(\tau)\bigr)\in \operatorname{Span}_{\mathbb Z}\{\operatorname{Lin}_{\varphi}(\nu): \nu\in\operatorname{Dec}_{\varphi}\text{ wide}\} \] for every wide \(\tau\in\operatorname{Dec}_{\widehat\varphi}\), where \(P\) kills the enlarged variables. This is not supplied.

Lemma 4.3 verifies only \(P(\operatorname{Lin}_{\widehat\varphi}(\widehat
u)) =\operatorname{Lin}_{\varphi}(
u)\) for originally indexed \(
u\); it does not control the additional wide enlarged equations. Therefore inconsistency of the enlarged system does not, by itself, imply inconsistency of the original subsystem. [doi:10.1112/jlms.12832, lines 777-818]

Conditional on the lower integral-basis result, conjugation is otherwise sound: \(\omega(s_\lambda)=s_{\lambda'}\) sends \(I_{r,q}\) to \(I_{q,r}\), preserves Schur degree and \(A_+\), and sends the interval above \(i^j\) to that above \(j^i\). The parameter translation \[ v^\vee=v_{q,\ q+j-i,\ q-i+1,\ n},\qquad (i^\vee,j^\vee,a^\vee,b^\vee)=(j,i,a,b) \] satisfies the bigrassmannian inequalities.

Under that conditional quotient isomorphism, conjugating \((j^i,\rho)\), \(\rho\subseteq b^a\), gives \[ (j^i,\rho)'=(i+\rho'_1,\ldots,i+\rho'_b,i^{\,j-b}), \] exactly the right-adjoined family. Its generation follows from graded Nakayama since \(A_+\) is nilpotent in \(\Lambda/I_{r,q}\).
